sourceUrl: https://arxiv.org/html/2601.01241v2 (v2, 22 Jun 2026 -- coded version; v1 also retrieved at https://arxiv.org/html/2601.01241v1; abstract page https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01241)
statedGuarantee: Untrusted third-party MCP tools can be executed for pre-adoption audit without granting them unconstrained host authority, and any case where authority-bearing bytes reach the agent's reasoning context is surfaced as auditable evidence. Two mechanisms carry this. (1) Containment: portable subjects run under a WASI backend that grants only selected environment variables, preopens one designated data directory, bounds captured stdout/stderr, and 'denies or mediates' network by default; unmodified servers instead run natively over stdio with no containment of their own. (2) Detection: a post-run, string-level 'witness' detector reports when environment, file, or tool-input canary bytes -- exact, separator-normalized, or base64/hex/ROT13-decoded -- appear inside an extracted LLM-visible sink (tool-result text, prompt/messages fields, structured return leaves), with network-intent/egress observations and declared-capability labels reported separately as weaker evidence classes.
advertisedRhetoric: v1: 'WASM offers a lightweight, capability-restricted runtime for containing untrusted code', and the stated goal 'Execute tools under least-privilege constraints (e.g., only a preopened /data directory, bounded outputs).' v2 softens this to an 'explicit capability interface': 'The WASI backend grants only selected environment variables, preopens a designated data directory, bounds captured standard output and standard error, and denies or mediates network behavior by default. This gives the scanner an explicit capability interface for pre-adoption behavioral auditing.' v2 also volunteers the retraction: "SandScope's contribution is therefore not 'WASM instead of OS sandboxing.'" On the detection side the paper claims no enforcement strength at all: 'SandScope is a positive-evidence detector, not a complete information-flow system.'
tierSpan: This native path provides protocol fidelity but does not by itself provide the same containment guarantees as WASI. In practice, native scans of untrusted tools should be paired with an OS-level sandbox such as Docker or Bubblewrap
cheapestDefeat: Two defeats, neither requiring a kernel bug or a WASM runtime escape. (a) Against containment: ship the tool as an ordinary native stdio MCP server rather than a portable WASM artifact. The paper states that path 'does not by itself provide the same containment guarantees as WASI', and that 'The real-world corpus primarily uses the native MCP path for unmodified servers.' Even in the controlled benchmark, 15 of 30 subjects were Native-only. No adversary work is required -- it is the default packaging of essentially every real MCP server, so the capability boundary is simply not on the path. (b) Against detection: never let source bytes traverse the analyzed chokepoint. Sinks are extracted only from captured stdout/stderr and JSON-RPC transcripts, so a tool that constructs a prompt without printing it, or that transforms the value by any means outside the four decoders (encryption, compression, hashing, summarization, custom encoding), emits no witness -- the paper states this itself. Both defeats bypass an application-level chokepoint over observed output; neither defeats an OS bound. Hence T3.
placementSpan: Our primary adversary controls content or arguments that reach an otherwise benign or trusted-but-risky MCP tool. Such inputs include user prompts, LLM-generated tool arguments, retrieved web pages, GitHub issues, README files, API responses, and dependency metadata.

coverageSpans.E1: The WASI backend grants only selected environment variables, preopens a designated data directory, bounds captured standard output and standard error, and denies or mediates network behavior by default. This gives the scanner an explicit capability interface for pre-adoption behavioral auditing.
coverageSpans.E2: The current taxonomy includes network access, browser automation, cloud or SaaS operation, filesystem access, code repository operation, database access, credential or secret handling, shell or process execution, and unknown or benign utility.
coverageSpans.E3: We also do not fully mediate arbitrary network behavior in the current prototype; instead, we treat network-like patterns as signals and leave full network syscall instrumentation as future work.
coverageSpans.E4: Each recovered tool is assigned zero or more capability labels. The current taxonomy includes network access, browser automation, cloud or SaaS operation, filesystem access, code repository operation, database access, credential or secret handling, shell or process execution, and unknown or benign utility.
coverageSpans.E5: Build failures, startup or protocol-initialization failures, and call-timeout failures reflect packaging conventions, runtime dependencies, server entry-point discovery, credential requirements, and protocol behavior.
coverageSpans.E6: SandScope seeds selected environment variables with unique canary values. These variables model secrets, tokens, user identifiers, local configuration, and private prompts that may be inherited by an MCP server from the host process.

schneider.surrogate: A single-trace, positive-evidence predicate a monitor can decide over one observed run: no source-derived snippet (full string, prefix/suffix/mid window; matched exactly, separator-normalized, or base64/hex/ROT13-decoded) occurs as a substring of any sink extracted from this run's stdout/stderr or JSON-RPC transcript. Plus, on the WASI path only, the genuine safety property that a file open must resolve to a preopened descriptor -- surfaced in v1 as 'failed to find a preopened file descriptor' errors.
schneider.objective: Absence of external-input-to-LLM-visible-sink flow: non-interference between authority-bearing sources (env secrets, mounted files, tool arguments, network content) and the agent's reasoning context. That is an information-flow hyperproperty, not decidable from any single trace, and the paper concedes exactly this: 'SandScope is a positive-evidence detector, not a complete information-flow system... Absence of a witness therefore does not prove absence of a flow.'

notes:
VERSION. Two versions exist and they are materially different systems. v1 (03 Jan 2026, ~9pp) is 'MCP-SandboxScan': WASI-only, three toy case studies, raw substring matching. v2 (22 Jun 2026, ~20pp) renames the system to 'SandScope' in the body while the arXiv title still reads 'MCP-SandboxScan', and adds a native stdio MCP execution path, a decoder-augmented witness detector, a 30-subject cross-language benchmark, an evasion benchmark, a 100-repo corpus, and a semantic capability profiler. I coded v2 as current; v1 is cited only where noted. Any coder who used v1 will produce a different and now-stale picture.

CATEGORY WARNING. This is an AUDIT/SCANNER paper, not an enforcement paper. Its product is a report, not a block. Nothing in the pipeline stops an effector at agent runtime; the only thing that actually denies an action is the WASI backend, and that only during a scan, only for portable subjects, and only against the scanner's own sandbox. Coding it on the action-surface grid is legitimate for the SoK's WASI question, but the grid systematically flatters it: most 'not-covered' cells are not failures of a control, they are effectors the paper never set out to bound.

WHAT THIS PAPER ANSWERS FOR THE SoK'S OPEN QUESTION (is WASM isolation a genuine T2 bound, or neither OS nor proxy?). The paper's own answer is the most useful datum in it, and it is negative on the strong reading. The authors explicitly refuse the framing that WASM substitutes for OS sandboxing -- "SandScope's contribution is therefore not 'WASM instead of OS sandboxing.'" -- and prescribe pairing native scans with Docker or Bubblewrap. Second, WASI turns out to be inapplicable to most real targets: 'The real-world corpus primarily uses the native MCP path for unmodified servers, while WASI is used when a portable artifact or shim is available,' and even in the hand-built controlled benchmark the execution-path split was Direct-Wasm 12 / Wasm-Shim 3 / Native-only 15 of 30. The paper also warns off reading its WASM-compatibility table as a measure of the boundary: 'The WASM-compatibility breakdown is an applicability observation rather than a measure of WASI effectiveness.' So: where WASI is on the path it behaves as a real capability boundary enforced below the tool's intent (v1 Case 3 shows blocked opens AND writes to /etc/passwd surfaced as runtime error evidence), but it is on the path for a minority of subjects and none of the paper's headline real-world results, and the authors themselves treat it as a backend to be composed with an OS sandbox rather than as the bound. Conservatively: this paper supplies no evidence that WASI alone carries a T2 claim for the MCP ecosystem, and supplies direct evidence that the deployed pipeline is T3.

TIER, WORKED. Guarantee: untrusted tools can be run for audit without host authority, and authority-bearing bytes reaching LLM-visible fields will be reported. Mechanism that must fail: either the WASI capability interface, or the stdout/transcript-derived sink extractor plus substring witness detector. Cheapest adversary action: do neither -- just be a normal native stdio MCP server (no containment, by the paper's own statement), and/or route the value through any channel or transform the extractor does not read. That defeats an application-layer chokepoint over observed output. T3. I considered T2 for the WASI-only subset and rejected it under the weakest-link rule, because the guarantee as evaluated is not confined to that subset.

COVERAGE REASONING.
E1 partial -- WASI preopen genuinely bounds file reads and writes for portable subjects (v1 Case 3: 'The execution output contains "failed to find a preopened file descriptor" errors for attempted read/write operations, including the system path attempt.'), but the native path is unbounded and the paper says so. Rename/unlink are never separately discussed.
E2 not-covered -- subprocess spawn is never mediated or even discussed as an effector; 'shell or process execution' appears only as one of nine SEMANTIC LABELS applied to 62 declared tools, i.e. attack-surface metadata, not a control. I deliberately did not credit WASI-preview1's absent process API, because the paper never states it: per the conservative stance, an interposition point the paper does not describe is unproven. A coder who credits that would score partial here; flag for adjudication.
E3 partial -- the gap is stated outright ('We also do not fully mediate arbitrary network behavior'). WASI 'denies or mediates network behavior by default' is itself ambiguous (denies OR mediates; the interposition point is not described), and everything else is intent-marker string matching plus optional egress monitoring: 'When an egress monitor or OS-level network policy is enabled, SandScope records denied connection attempts as host-and-port observations. Otherwise, network evidence is limited to explicit fetch or egress intents that surface in captured artifacts.' Descendant egress is nowhere addressed, which caps at partial regardless. Note that both controlled false negatives were C2-beacon subjects -- the covert-egress case is exactly where the detector missed.
E4 not-covered -- VCS push never appears as an effector; 'code repository operation' is a declared-capability label on 198 tools.
E5 not-covered -- and this is the cell an adjudicator should look at hardest. The scanner ITSELF installs and builds 91 third-party repositories on the audit host in order to scan them (19 build failures and 31 startup failures are reported), with no containment described for the build step and no mention of install hooks. Running npm/pip installs across 91 untrusted repos is an unmediated E5 executed by the very tool that exists to contain untrusted code. The paper does not acknowledge this.
E6 partial -- WASI allowlists environment variables ('grants only selected environment variables'), a real restriction for portable subjects; the native path inherits host env. Detection-side, credentials are modeled as seeded canaries, not a published credential list, and keychain / config-file / cloud-metadata-endpoint credentials are entirely out of scope. Per the E6 rule (undefined list caps at partial) this cannot exceed partial even for the WASI path.
E7 not-covered -- sub-agent spawn is not addressed anywhere; no span exists, hence an empty span field.

COVERT-CHANNEL RULE APPLIED. Every honest exclusion the paper documents still scores partial or worse, never covered: 'The detector covers exact substrings, suffix-aware snippets, separator-normalized chunking, and a small set of decoder passes, but does not infer arbitrary transformations such as encryption, compression, hashing, semantic rewriting, summarization, or custom encodings.' The honesty is exemplary and changes nothing about the cell.

EVIDENCE GRADE -- where I hesitated. L2 is defensible and I chose it; L3 is arguable. For L3: the released fixtures include an evasion benchmark whose 'Raw-only detected = no' rows (rot13 / hex / base64 / chunked) are a reproducible bypass of the shipped v1 detector, and v1 Table III records base64 -> observed no-flow. Against L3: v2's enhanced detector closes exactly those four transforms, and the residual bypass classes (encryption, compression, hashing, semantic rewriting) are ASSERTED rather than exercised with a fixture; likewise the containment bypass (use the native path) is documented by the authors but never demonstrated as an attack. The strongest reproducible bypass in v2 is therefore against a baseline the paper itself replaces. L2.

ADVERSARY PLACEMENT -- where I hesitated. The paper NAMES A2 as primary ('attacker-controlled external content or LLM-generated arguments'), and the real-world targeted pass does test it by seeding MCP_INPUT_CANARY_* into schema-generated arguments and observing reflection (Repo B). But roughly half the controlled benchmark subjects are deliberately malicious fixtures -- env leaks, file-exfiltration, C2 beacons -- which is A5 (supply chain), and the paper calls that its declared secondary adversary: 'Malicious or compromised MCP servers are a secondary supply-chain threat.' An adjudicator could reasonably flip primary to A5 on the 'what does the evaluation actually test' criterion. I kept A2 primary because the paper declares it, the headline real-world result (60 witnesses across 12 repos) is A2-shaped, and the confused-deputy framing is the whole thesis. A1 is secondary only in the weak sense that the scanner is a pre-adoption vetting gate against an outside supplier.

OTHER NUMBERS WORTH CARRYING INTO THE SoK. Real-world applicability is the quiet result: of 100 repos, 91 resolved, 35 completed a shallow scan (38.5%), 33 re-executed under targeted exploration, and only 12 produced any witness at all. Tier-2 (MCP-adjacent) coverage was 14.3%. Precision 1.000 / recall 0.889 / F1 0.941 is measured on 30 authors-built controlled subjects, NOT on the corpus -- do not quote those figures as real-world detection rates. The semantic profiler's 886/1127 'security-sensitive declared capability' figure is self-declared metadata, explicitly not a vulnerability claim ('We interpret these labels as declared attack surface and test-prioritization evidence, not as vulnerability findings'), and the cross-validation table shows 14 repos with declared egress risk never exercised and 4 repos with observed egress that metadata missed -- declared capability and actual behavior diverge in both directions.

CODE AVAILABILITY. Released only as an anonymized 4open.science mirror (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MCP-SandboxScan-FFFB) in both versions, so the artifact could not be independently exercised for this coding; all grading is from the text.
